subject: physics

items.q: Which statement defines a longitudinal wave?
items.correct: A wave in which the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
items.misconception: A wave in which the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
items.why: Both words are new and abstract. Textbook diagrams of a longitudinal wave on a slinky show the coils as vertical lines bunched along the spring, which invites students to read the vertical lines as vertical motion. Longitudinal: oscillation along the direction of travel (sound, P-waves, a slinky pushed and pulled). Transverse: oscillation across the direction of travel (string, S-waves, electromagnetic waves). Anchor each definition to a physical example rather than to the word.
items.random_wrong: A wave in which the particles of the medium travel along with it, carrying the energy with them

items.q: A transverse wave travels in the +x direction along a stretched rope. At one instant, the graph of the displacement y of the rope (upwards positive) against position x is a sine curve: y = 0 at x = 0, y = +2.0 cm at x = 0.25 m, y = 0 at x = 0.50 m, y = −2.0 cm at x = 0.75 m and y = 0 at x = 1.00 m. How is the point of the rope at x = 0.50 m moving at this instant?
items.correct: Upwards (+y), at its maximum speed
items.misconception: Downwards (−y), at its maximum speed
items.why: The graph looks exactly like a drawing of a rope, and students read graphs as pictures of motion ('graph as picture' errors are well documented in kinematics). Following the curve forwards seems natural because the wave moves forwards. To find the direction of motion of a particle, shift the whole curve a little in the direction of travel and see whether the displacement at that particle's position increases or decreases. A particle just ahead of a crest is about to be reached by the crest, so it is moving towards positive displacement.
items.random_wrong: Neither way: it is momentarily at rest

items.q: A longitudinal wave travels in the +x direction along a slinky spring. Displacements of the coils in the +x direction are positive. At one instant, the graph of displacement s against equilibrium position x is a sine curve: s = 0 at x = 0, s = +3.0 mm at x = 10 cm, s = 0 at x = 20 cm, s = −3.0 mm at x = 30 cm and s = 0 at x = 40 cm. Where, between x = 0 and x = 40 cm, is the centre of a compression?
items.correct: At x = 20 cm, where coils on both sides are displaced towards it
items.misconception: At x = 10 cm, where the displacement is greatest and positive
items.why:
Many textbook diagrams draw a longitudinal wave directly above a sine curve with the compressions lined up with the crests; that curve is a graph of pressure or density, not displacement. Students transfer the alignment to displacement graphs. Work from the particles: at a compression the particles on the left have been displaced forwards (+) and those on the right backwards (−), so the compression is where the displacement graph crosses zero going from + to −. The crest (maximum displacement) is a quarter-wavelength away from both the compression and the rarefaction.

Working: Wavelength = 40 cm (s = 0 → +max → 0 → −max → 0 between x = 0 and 40 cm). Just below x = 20 cm, s > 0: coils displaced in +x, towards 20 cm. Just above x = 20 cm, s < 0: coils displaced in −x, also towards 20 cm. So the coils crowd together at x = 20 cm (compression). At x = 0 and x = 40 cm the neighbours are displaced away from the point (rarefactions). At x = 10 cm and 30 cm neighbouring coils have almost equal displacements, so the spacing there is almost normal.
items.random_wrong: At x = 10 cm and x = 30 cm, where s has its greatest magnitude
items.working: Wavelength = 40 cm (s = 0 → +max → 0 → −max → 0 between x = 0 and 40 cm). Just below x = 20 cm, s > 0: coils displaced in +x, towards 20 cm. Just above x = 20 cm, s < 0: coils displaced in −x, also towards 20 cm. So the coils crowd together at x = 20 cm (compression). At x = 0 and x = 40 cm the neighbours are displaced away from the point (rarefactions). At x = 10 cm and 30 cm neighbouring coils have almost equal displacements, so the spacing there is almost normal.

items.q: A student flicks one end of a long, horizontal, stretched rope once, and a single transverse pulse travels along it. A ribbon tied to the rope halfway along moves up and then back down to its original position as the pulse passes. Which statement about the pulse is correct?
items.correct: It transferred energy along the rope, although the rope had no net displacement.
items.misconception: It transferred no energy past the ribbon, since the rope there ended where it started.
items.why: Students link energy transfer with something being carried, like a delivery. If no material ends up anywhere new, it seems nothing can have been transferred. Energy can be transferred by a chain of interactions without any material travelling: each section of the medium does work on the next. A pulse sent along a rope can make the far end jerk up and do work, although no part of the rope has moved along it.
items.random_wrong: It transferred energy by carrying sections of the rope along with it to the far end.

items.q: A transverse wave travels along a stretched string. Adjacent crests are 1.2 m apart. A graph of displacement y against time t for one point on the string is a sine curve: y = 0 at t = 0, y is a maximum at t = 5 ms, y = 0 at t = 10 ms, y is a minimum at t = 15 ms and y = 0 at t = 20 ms, after which the pattern repeats. What is the wave speed?
items.correct: 60 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 120 m s⁻¹
items.why:
A sine curve seems to 'start again' at each zero crossing, and each half-cycle looks like a complete hump. The same error appears in space as taking the distance between successive zero points as the wavelength. One cycle includes a crest AND a trough. Measure T between successive crests, or between alternate zero crossings (where the curve crosses in the same direction).

Working: From the displacement–time graph, one complete oscillation (0 → maximum → 0 → minimum → 0) takes T = 20 ms = 0.020 s. Adjacent crests give λ = 1.2 m. v = λ/T = 1.2 m / 0.020 s = 60 m s⁻¹ (equivalently f = 1/T = 50 Hz and v = fλ = 50 Hz × 1.2 m = 60 m s⁻¹).
items.specStatementText: wavelength λ, frequency f, time period T, and wave speed v applied to wave motion as given by v = fλ = λ/T
items.working: From the displacement–time graph, one complete oscillation (0 → maximum → 0 → minimum → 0) takes T = 20 ms = 0.020 s. Adjacent crests give λ = 1.2 m. v = λ/T = 1.2 m / 0.020 s = 60 m s⁻¹ (equivalently f = 1/T = 50 Hz and v = fλ = 50 Hz × 1.2 m = 60 m s⁻¹).

items.q: A vibrator sends a continuous transverse wave along a stretched string. The student increases the amplitude of the vibrator's oscillation but keeps its frequency and the tension in the string the same. What happens to the wave speed and to the wavelength?
items.correct: The speed and the wavelength both stay the same, as f and the string are unchanged
items.misconception: Both increase, as a larger amplitude makes the wave move faster along the string
items.why: In everyday life 'more effort' makes things move faster (throw harder, the ball goes faster). Physics education research on waves on strings finds that many students predict a larger flick sends a pulse faster. Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium only. Doubling the amplitude of a pulse on a rope leaves its travel time unchanged; the extra energy goes into larger oscillations of each part of the rope.
items.specStatementText: wavelength λ, frequency f, time period T, and wave speed v applied to wave motion as given by v = fλ = λ/T
items.random_wrong: The speed is unchanged; the wavelength is longer, as the wave is now bigger

items.q: A student measures the wavelength λ of waves on one stretched string at three frequencies f of the vibrator, keeping the tension constant: f = 20 Hz, λ = 1.50 m; f = 40 Hz, λ = 0.75 m; f = 60 Hz, λ = 0.50 m. Which conclusion do the data support?
items.correct: The speed is the same at each frequency, so it does not depend on the frequency.
items.misconception: The speed rises with frequency, because v = fλ and f was increased each time.
items.why:
v = fλ is read as a formula for v in which f can be changed while λ stays fixed. In everyday language 'faster' vibrations suggest a faster wave. The medium sets the speed (for a string, its tension and mass per unit length). The source sets the frequency. The wavelength then adjusts: λ = v/f. Measurements at several frequencies on one string give the same value of fλ.

Working: v = fλ: 20 Hz × 1.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 40 Hz × 0.75 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 60 Hz × 0.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹. The speed is constant; λ is inversely proportional to f.
items.specStatementText: wavelength λ, frequency f, time period T, and wave speed v applied to wave motion as given by v = fλ = λ/T
items.random_wrong: The speed falls as the frequency rises, because the period rises as frequency does.
items.working: v = fλ: 20 Hz × 1.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 40 Hz × 0.75 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 60 Hz × 0.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹. The speed is constant; λ is inversely proportional to f.

items.q: Which statement describes the nature of a sound wave travelling through air?
items.correct: A longitudinal wave in which air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
items.misconception: A transverse wave in which air particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
items.why: Sound is usually displayed as a transverse-looking trace on an oscilloscope or drawn as a sine curve, and students take the picture literally. The trace is a graph of pressure (or displacement) against time, not a picture of the wave. The loudspeaker cone moves back and forth along the direction of travel, pushing and pulling on the air in front of it. The air particles move the same way, creating regions of higher and lower pressure that travel outward. An oscilloscope trace plots that variation against time.
items.random_wrong: A flow of air particles from the source to the ear, carrying the energy along with them

items.q: A loudspeaker emits a steady sound of frequency 500 Hz towards a listener 10 m away. Ignoring random thermal motion, which describes the motion of a particle of air midway between them while the sound passes?
items.correct: It oscillates about a fixed position, back and forth along the line to the listener.
items.misconception: It travels from the loudspeaker to the listener at the speed of sound in air.
items.why:
People feel moving air near a loudspeaker or a shout, and speak of sound 'coming out of' things or 'filling' a room. Physics education research on sound documents the view of sound as a travelling entity or substance. If air flowed from a speaker at the speed of sound there would be a gale of 340 m s⁻¹. A candle flame in front of a loudspeaker flickers back and forth; it is not blown steadily away. Only energy and the disturbance travel.

Working: Sound in air is longitudinal, so each air particle oscillates about its own equilibrium position along the direction of travel (along the line to the listener), with no net displacement. It oscillates at the source frequency, 500 Hz, so T = 1/f = 1/(500 Hz) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s (not 500 s).
items.random_wrong: It oscillates about a fixed position, at right angles to the line to the listener.
items.working: Sound in air is longitudinal, so each air particle oscillates about its own equilibrium position along the direction of travel (along the line to the listener), with no net displacement. It oscillates at the source frequency, 500 Hz, so T = 1/f = 1/(500 Hz) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s (not 500 s).

items.q: A student at one end of a long steel railway track puts an ear to the rail. At the other end, 1.0 km away, the rail is struck once with a hammer. The student hears two separate sounds, 0.20 s and 2.9 s after the blow. Which conclusion do these observations support?
items.correct: Sound travels faster in steel than in air: the first sound came through the rail.
items.misconception: Sound is slowed by closely packed particles: the first sound came through the air.
items.why:
Solids feel like barriers: walls muffle sound, so solids seem to impede it. Students picture particles as obstacles to be pushed past rather than as links that pass the disturbance along. Sound is passed along by forces between neighbouring particles. In a solid these forces are strong and the particles are strongly coupled, so the disturbance is passed on quickly. Muffling by a wall is due mainly to reflection at its surfaces and absorption inside it, not to slow travel through it.

Working: Distance = 1.0 × 10³ m by both paths. Speed via first sound = 1.0 × 10³ m / 0.20 s = 5.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (steel). Speed via second sound = 1.0 × 10³ m / 2.9 s ≈ 3.4 × 10² m s⁻¹ (air).
items.random_wrong: Sound has one fixed speed, so the second sound was an echo of the first sound.
items.working: Distance = 1.0 × 10³ m by both paths. Speed via first sound = 1.0 × 10³ m / 0.20 s = 5.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (steel). Speed via second sound = 1.0 × 10³ m / 2.9 s ≈ 3.4 × 10² m s⁻¹ (air).

items.q: Which statement describes the nature of electromagnetic waves?
items.correct: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
items.misconception: Oscillations of the particles of the medium they travel through, so they cannot cross a vacuum
items.why: Students generalise from sound, water waves and waves on strings, which are all met first and all need a medium. Historically, physicists also assumed a medium (the 'ether') for light. Light from the Sun and stars crosses millions of kilometres of empty space. A lamp inside an evacuated jar can still be seen. Only mechanical waves need a medium.
items.random_wrong: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel faster in a vacuum the higher their frequency

items.q: Which list places the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength?
items.correct: gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
items.misconception: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
items.why: The spectrum is usually listed from radio waves to gamma rays, in order of increasing frequency, and students assume the list is in increasing order of everything. 'Bigger' frequency seems to go with 'bigger' wavelength. Use fλ = c: if f increases along the list, λ must decrease. Radio waves have wavelengths of metres or more; gamma rays about 10⁻¹² m or less.
items.random_wrong: gamma, X-ray, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, microwave, radio

items.q: In a vacuum, the radio waves from an FM radio station have a wavelength of 3.0 m, and the X-rays used in medical imaging have a wavelength of about 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. How do their frequencies compare?
items.correct: The X-ray frequency is 3 × 10¹⁰ times the radio frequency, since f = c/λ.
items.misconception: The X-ray frequency is higher, because X-rays travel faster than radio waves.
items.why:
Higher-frequency radiation is described as more energetic and more penetrating, and in mechanics more energy often means more speed. v = fλ is also read as v ∝ f. In a vacuum every region of the spectrum travels at c; the regions differ only in frequency and wavelength. Higher f means shorter λ, with fλ = c. Measurements of c made with radio waves, microwaves and visible light all give the same value, 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

Working: In a vacuum both travel at c, so f = c/λ. f(radio) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ / 3.0 m = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz. f(X-ray) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Ratio = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ / 1.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10¹⁰ (= 3.0 m / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
items.random_wrong: The radio frequency is 3 × 10¹⁰ times the X-ray frequency, since f rises with λ.
items.working: In a vacuum both travel at c, so f = c/λ. f(radio) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ / 3.0 m = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz. f(X-ray) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Ratio = 3.0 × 10¹⁸ / 1.0 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10¹⁰ (= 3.0 m / 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).

items.q: An electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar and can be both seen and heard. A pump gradually removes the air from the jar while the bell keeps working. Which prediction, with its explanation, is correct?
items.correct: The sound fades but the bell stays visible: light, unlike sound, needs no medium.
items.misconception: Neither changes, because sound, like light, can travel through an evacuated jar.
items.why: Films show loud explosions in space, and students know that all waves carry energy, so they assume every wave can cross empty space. Sound needs particles to oscillate. As air is pumped out of a jar containing a ringing bell, the sound fades although the bell can still be seen: light, an electromagnetic wave, needs no medium.
items.specStatementText: the differences between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.
items.random_wrong: The sound fades and the bell vanishes from view, since both waves need air to travel.

items.q: Which statement describes a difference between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves?
items.correct: Mechanical waves need a material medium; electromagnetic waves can also travel through a vacuum.
items.misconception: Mechanical waves are longitudinal waves, whereas electromagnetic waves are transverse.
items.why: The standard pair of examples is 'light (transverse)' and 'sound (longitudinal)', and the two classifications, transverse/longitudinal and electromagnetic/mechanical, are merged into one. Keep the two classifications separate. Transverse or longitudinal describes the direction of oscillation. Mechanical or electromagnetic describes what oscillates. A guitar string carries a transverse mechanical wave; sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave; light is a transverse electromagnetic wave.
items.specStatementText: the differences between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.
items.random_wrong: Mechanical waves change speed between media; electromagnetic waves keep speed c in all.

items.q: The graph shows the displacement y of a stretched rope against position x at one instant, as a transverse wave travels along the rope in the direction of the arrow (towards −x). P is a point on the rope. How is P moving at this instant?
items.correct: Downwards, in the −y direction
items.misconception: At rest: its displacement is zero
items.why: Displacement and velocity are confused, as in kinematics where students assume a body at x = 0 must have v = 0. On a snapshot graph the curve 'sits on the axis' at that point, which looks like rest. The particles of a wave oscillate like simple harmonic oscillators: speed is greatest at the equilibrium position (zero displacement) and zero at the extremes (maximum displacement). A displacement graph shows where particles are, not how fast they are moving.
items.random_wrong: Upwards, in the +y direction

figure.alt: Displacement–position graph: displacement y (vertical axis, upwards positive) against position x for a stretched rope at one instant. The curve is a sine wave over one and a half wavelengths starting at y = 0 at x = 0. A red arrow above the curve labelled 'wave velocity' points to the left, towards −x. A red dot labelled P marks a point where the curve crosses the x axis (y = 0) going downwards: the crest is to the left of P and the trough to the right of P. The origin is marked 0.

items.q: The graph shows the displacement y of one point on a stretched rope against time t as a transverse wave passes along the rope. Which describes the motion of this point at the instant t₁ marked on the graph?
items.correct: Moving upwards at its maximum speed
items.misconception: Moving downwards at its maximum speed
items.why: Both graphs have the same sine shape, and textbooks often show a sinusoidal curve labelled simply 'a wave'. Students read whichever graph is in front of them as an image of the string and take the horizontal repeat as a length. Check the horizontal axis first. Position x gives a snapshot: the repeat distance is λ, and a point's motion is found by shifting the curve in the direction of travel. Time t gives the history of one point: the repeat distance is T, and the point's velocity is the gradient of the curve.
items.random_wrong: At rest, because its displacement is zero

figure.alt: Displacement–time graph: displacement y (vertical axis, upwards positive) against time t for one point on a stretched rope. The curve is a sine wave starting at y = 0 at t = 0, rising to a crest, falling through zero to a trough, and repeating for about one and a half cycles. A dashed red vertical line marks the instant t₁, where the curve crosses the t axis (y = 0) with the trough before t₁ and the crest after t₁. The origin is marked 0.

items.q: A transverse wave travels along a string. Graph 1 shows the displacement y against position x along the string at one instant. Graph 2 shows the displacement y of one point on the string against time t. What is the speed of the wave?
items.correct: 6.0 m s⁻¹
items.why:
Both describe 'how the oscillation repeats' and both are read from the same displacement–time graph. Students who learn v = fλ and v = λ/T side by side can substitute T where f belongs. Frequency counts oscillations per second; period is seconds per oscillation. Doubling f halves T. Write the units: v = fλ has (s⁻¹)(m) = m s⁻¹, whereas T × λ would have units s m, which is not a speed.

Working: Graph 1 is a snapshot: its repeat distance is the wavelength. The pattern repeats every 0.60 m (zero crossings at 0, 0.30 m and 0.60 m are half a wavelength apart), so λ = 0.60 m. Graph 2 is the history of one point: its repeat time is the period. The displacement repeats every 0.10 s (zero crossings at 0.05 s and 0.10 s are half a period apart), so T = 0.10 s. v = λ/T = 0.60 m / 0.10 s = 6.0 m s⁻¹ (equivalently f = 1/T = 10 Hz and v = fλ = 10 Hz × 0.60 m = 6.0 m s⁻¹).
items.specStatementText: wavelength λ, frequency f, time period T, and wave speed v applied to wave motion as given by v = fλ = λ/T
items.random_wrong: 12 m s⁻¹
items.working: Graph 1 is a snapshot: its repeat distance is the wavelength. The pattern repeats every 0.60 m (zero crossings at 0, 0.30 m and 0.60 m are half a wavelength apart), so λ = 0.60 m. Graph 2 is the history of one point: its repeat time is the period. The displacement repeats every 0.10 s (zero crossings at 0.05 s and 0.10 s are half a period apart), so T = 0.10 s. v = λ/T = 0.60 m / 0.10 s = 6.0 m s⁻¹ (equivalently f = 1/T = 10 Hz and v = fλ = 10 Hz × 0.60 m = 6.0 m s⁻¹).

figure.alt: Two graphs. Graph 1: displacement y / cm against position x / m along the string at one instant; the curve is a sine wave starting at y = 0 at x = 0, with zero crossings at 0.30 m, 0.60 m and 0.90 m, so one and a half repeats fill 0 to 0.90 m. Graph 2: displacement y / cm against time t / s for one point on the string; the curve is a sine wave starting at y = 0 at t = 0 with zero crossings at 0.05 s, 0.10 s, 0.15 s and 0.20 s, so two full repeats fill 0 to 0.20 s. Both curves have the same amplitude; no amplitude value is marked.

items.q: The graph shows the displacement s of the air particles against position x at one instant as a sound wave travels through air along the x direction. Displacements in the +x direction are positive. Four positions P, Q, R and S are marked on the graph. Which position is at the centre of a rarefaction?
items.correct: Point S
items.misconception: Point P
items.why: Students learn the partial rule 'compressions are at zero displacement' and apply it to every zero crossing, without checking the direction in which the neighbouring particles have moved. Check the signs on either side of each zero crossing. Crossing from + to − (neighbours displaced towards the point) gives a compression; crossing from − to + (neighbours displaced away) gives a rarefaction. Adjacent compressions are one wavelength apart, not half a wavelength.
items.random_wrong: Point Q

figure.alt: Displacement–position graph for a sound wave: displacement s of the air particles (vertical axis, positive for displacement in the +x direction) against position x. The curve is a sine wave over one and a half wavelengths starting at s = 0 at x = 0. Four positions are marked with red dots: P at the first crest (maximum positive s), Q at the next zero crossing where s falls from positive to negative, R at the trough (maximum negative s), and S at the following zero crossing where s rises from negative to positive. The origin is marked 0.

items.q: The diagram shows the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum on a logarithmic scale of wavelength λ. A wave has a wavelength of 2 × 10⁻⁵ m. In which region of the spectrum shown does it lie?
items.correct: the infrared region
items.misconception: the ultraviolet region
items.why: The prefixes are remembered but not what they refer to: 'infra' (below) and 'ultra' (beyond) describe frequency relative to red and violet light, and students attach them to wavelength or swap them. Infra-red = below red in frequency, so longer in wavelength than red light (about 700 nm). Ultra-violet = beyond violet in frequency, so shorter in wavelength than violet light (about 400 nm).
items.random_wrong: the microwave region

items.q: A small loudspeaker emitting a steady note and a lamp are sealed inside a glass jar. Outside the jar a microphone and a light sensor face them. At t = 0 a pump starts removing the air from the jar. The graph shows the output of each sensor against time. Which conclusion do the two traces support?
items.correct: The sound wave needs a material medium to reach the microphone, but the light wave does not.
items.misconception: The pump drew the sound out of the jar along with the air that was carrying it.
items.why: People feel moving air near a loudspeaker or a shout, and speak of sound 'coming out of' things or 'filling' a room. Physics education research on sound documents the view of sound as a travelling entity or substance. If air flowed from a speaker at the speed of sound there would be a gale of 340 m s⁻¹. A candle flame in front of a loudspeaker flickers back and forth; it is not blown steadily away. Only energy and the disturbance travel.
items.specStatementText: the differences between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.
items.random_wrong: Both waves need air, but the light needed only the trace of air the pump left behind.

figure.alt: Graph of sensor output (vertical axis, no scale) against time t / s (horizontal axis, marked 0, 20, 40, 60). The pump starts at t = 0. The trace labelled 'light sensor' is a horizontal straight line at a high, constant value from t = 0 to t = 60 s. The trace labelled 'microphone' starts at a moderate value at t = 0, falls steadily, is close to zero by about t = 40 s and stays at zero to t = 60 s.

items.q: When a wave travels through a medium, do the particles of the medium travel along with the wave?
items.correct: No. Each particle oscillates about its own fixed equilibrium position. The wave shape and the energy travel; the medium has no resultant displacement.
items.misconception: The particles of the medium are carried along by the wave, so a wave transports material from the source towards the receiver.
items.why: Everyday experience of breaking sea waves and of wind carrying things suggests that waves move matter, and the word 'travel' is naturally applied to the stuff rather than to the pattern. Diagrams show the wave moving without showing that individual particles stay put. Follow one particle rather than the wave: in a transverse wave it moves up and down about a fixed point, in a longitudinal wave back and forth about a fixed point. After the wave has passed, it is where it started. What travels is the disturbance, and with it energy.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the medium most compressed where the particles have the largest displacement?
items.correct: No. How compressed the medium is depends on how much neighbouring particles are displaced relative to each other, not on how far each one has moved. Where displacement is largest (at a crest or trough of the graph) neighbouring particles are displaced by nearly the same amount, so the spacing is nearly normal.
items.misconception: The medium is most compressed wherever the particles have been displaced furthest from equilibrium, in either direction.
items.why: 'Displaced' and 'squashed' feel like the same thing: a particle that has moved a long way seems to have been pushed hardest. Displacement is conflated with density or pressure. Compression means particles closer together. That happens where particles behind are displaced forwards and particles ahead are displaced backwards, i.e. where the displacement changes most steeply from + to −, which is at a point of zero displacement.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a longitudinal wave simply one that travels along the length of a long object such as a spring or rope?
items.correct: No. The classification depends on the direction of oscillation relative to the direction of energy transfer, not on the shape of the medium. A wave along a rope that is shaken sideways is transverse; the same spring can carry transverse or longitudinal waves.
items.misconception: A longitudinal wave is any wave that travels along the length of a long medium, such as a spring or a rope.
items.why: 'Longitudinal' literally means 'lengthwise', and the first examples students meet (slinky springs, ropes) are long objects that the wave travels along. Ask: which way do the particles move compared with the direction the energy goes? Parallel = longitudinal; perpendicular = transverse. Every travelling wave travels along its medium, so that cannot distinguish the two types.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a time read in milliseconds be substituted directly into v = λ/T or f = 1/T?
items.correct: No. SI units must be used: 20 ms = 0.020 s. Otherwise the speed comes out 1000 times too small (or the frequency 1000 times too small).
items.misconception: A time given in milliseconds can be substituted into the wave equation without converting it to seconds.
items.why: Graph axes labelled 't / ms' make the numbers easy to read off, and the prefix is lost when the number is carried into the equation. This is a systematic procedural error rather than a belief about waves. Convert every quantity to SI units before substituting: 1 ms = 1 × 10⁻³ s. Then check the answer is physically sensible; a wave on a string does not travel at a few centimetres per second.
items.specStatementText: wavelength λ, frequency f, time period T, and wave speed v applied to wave motion as given by v = fλ = λ/T
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does increasing the amplitude of a wave increase its wavelength?
items.correct: No. Amplitude (the maximum displacement) and wavelength (the distance between adjacent crests) are independent. For a given frequency and medium, λ = v/f is unchanged whatever the amplitude.
items.misconception: A larger amplitude makes a 'bigger' wave, so its wavelength increases too.
items.why: Students think of the 'size' of a wave as a single property, so taller waves seem longer as well. On a graph, amplitude and wavelength are both lengths. Amplitude is measured perpendicular to the axis (or along the displacement direction); wavelength along the direction of travel. The wavelength depends only on v and f: λ = v/f.

items.q: If the source of a wave oscillates with a larger amplitude, does the frequency increase?
items.correct: No. Frequency is the number of oscillations per second. A source can oscillate with a larger amplitude at the same frequency; its parts then move faster, but it does not complete more cycles per second.
items.misconception: A source that oscillates with a larger amplitude is moving faster, so it produces a shorter wavelength; the speed of the source's motion is confused with its rate of oscillation.
items.why: Moving a hand further in the same time means moving it faster, and 'faster shaking' is how frequency is described informally. The speed of the source is confused with its rate of oscillation. Separate how far (amplitude) from how often (frequency). A signal generator can change one without the other. With the frequency and the medium unchanged, λ = v/f is unchanged.

items.q: Does sound have one fixed speed in every material?
items.correct: No. The speed of sound depends on the medium (and, in a gas, on temperature): about 340 m s⁻¹ in air, 1500 m s⁻¹ in water and 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel.
items.misconception: Sound has a single fixed speed, 'the speed of sound', which is the same whatever it travels through.
items.why: The phrase 'the speed of sound' and the single value 340 m s⁻¹ used in almost every school problem suggest a universal constant, by analogy with the speed of light. The speed of any mechanical wave is set by its medium. 'The speed of sound' in problems means the speed in air under stated conditions. In water and in solids the speed is several times larger.

items.q: Are electromagnetic waves streams of charged particles, like some nuclear radiation?
items.correct: No. Electromagnetic waves are oscillations of electric and magnetic fields. They carry no charge and are not streams of charged particles, unlike alpha and beta radiation.
items.misconception: Electromagnetic radiation is a stream of tiny charged particles given out by the source, the same kind of thing as alpha and beta radiation.
items.why: The single word 'radiation' is used both for electromagnetic waves and for alpha and beta particles, and all of them are met in the context of hazards, so they are lumped together. Alpha and beta radiation are charged particles emitted by nuclei; they are deflected by electric and magnetic fields. Electromagnetic waves are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields, uncharged and undeflected by such fields.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do microwaves have shorter wavelengths than infrared radiation?
items.correct: No. Microwaves have wavelengths of order 10⁻² m, longer than infrared (about 10⁻⁵ m) and visible light; only radio waves are longer. They are "micro" only compared with radio waves.
items.misconception: Microwaves have very short, micrometre-scale wavelengths, so they lie on the short-wavelength side of infrared, between visible light and infrared.
items.why: The prefix "micro" suggests micrometres, and the name is taken to describe the wavelength in absolute terms rather than in comparison with radio waves. Microwave wavelengths are of order centimetres (a microwave oven uses about 12 cm). The name distinguishes them from the longer radio waves. In order of increasing wavelength microwaves come just before radio waves.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, c, in every medium?
items.correct: No. c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ is the speed in a vacuum (and almost the same in air). In glass or water light travels more slowly, which is why it refracts.
items.misconception: Electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, c, in every medium, so only mechanical waves change speed from one medium to another.
items.why: c is called 'the speed of light' and is presented as a universal constant, without the words 'in a vacuum'. The speed of light in water is about 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and in glass about 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Both mechanical and electromagnetic waves change speed between media; only in a vacuum do all electromagnetic waves share the speed c.
items.specStatementText: the differences between mechanical waves and electromagnetic waves.

items.q: Roughly what range of wavelengths does visible light occupy on the electromagnetic spectrum?
items.correct: About 4 × 10⁻⁷ m (violet) to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m (red): less than one order of magnitude, a thin sliver on a logarithmic scale between the ultraviolet and infrared regions.
items.misconception: Visible light occupies a broad band in the middle of the spectrum, extending to wavelengths of tens of micrometres or more.
items.why: Spectrum diagrams expand the visible region into a wide rainbow strip so that the colours can be shown, and everyday experience gives no sense of scale for light; students carry the width of the drawing over to the wavelength scale. On a logarithmic wavelength scale the visible band is narrower than any other region, about a quarter of a decade wide. Wavelengths from about 10⁻⁶ m up to 10⁻³ m are infrared, however close to the red end they look on a drawing.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On a displacement-position graph of a longitudinal wave, which zero crossings are compressions and which are rarefactions?
items.correct: Where s falls through zero (positive just to the left, negative just to the right) the neighbours on both sides are displaced towards the point: a compression. Where s rises through zero they are displaced away from it: a rarefaction.
items.misconception: Where the displacement graph falls through zero the particles have thinned out (a rarefaction) and where it rises through zero they have bunched up (a compression): the two kinds of zero crossing are attached the wrong way round.
items.why: Students learn that compressions and rarefactions sit at the zero crossings but do not work through the sign convention particle by particle: a falling curve suggests "less" or "spreading out" and a rising curve "more" or "building up", so the labels are swapped. Check the neighbours. On a falling crossing the particle just to the left has moved in +x (towards the point) and the one just to the right in -x (also towards it): a compression. On a rising crossing both have moved away: a rarefaction.
